792.title: Damayanti in the forest
792.hook: Damayanti wakes alone in half a cloth, and her dharma is all she has left in the forest
792.carry: dharma protects the one who protects it
792.howItsDone: Damayanti's wandering, from the forest to the court of Chedi, is told in the Nala story of the Mahabharata's Vana Parva; many teachers read it alongside the well-known line dharmo rakshati rakshitah, dharma protects the one who protects it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vastra, the one cloth Nala and Damayanti shared, until he cut it in the dark and left. Your line was partners in dharma share the one cloth.

Half a cloth. That's what Damayanti finds when she wakes on the floor of the empty rest house. Half of the garment they shared, and no husband. She calls his name. She runs through the trees calling it, half thinking he's hiding, playing some cruel game. Come out, she says, I'm frightened. Nobody answers. Only the trees, and the empty road, and her own voice coming back. And the story, which has followed Nala until now, turns and follows her.
screen: `HALF A CLOTH.` → `SHE CALLS HIS NAME.` → `THE STORY FOLLOWS HER.`

segments.voice: Her first thought, the story says, is for him: who will look after him now, hungry and alone? Then the forest closes in. A huge serpent seizes her, and even in its coils she cries out for Nala, not for herself. A hunter kills the snake and frees her, then looks at her the wrong way. Damayanti has nothing left: no husband, no kingdom, half a cloth. But she still has her faithfulness, and she calls on it. The hunter falls dead. She walks on and asks everything she meets. A mountain. Ascetics, who promise she'll see Nala again and then vanish, hermitage and all. An Ashoka tree in bloom, whose name means without sorrow: live up to your name, she begs it, and take mine. At last she reaches the city of Chedi, ragged, and the queen mother takes her in. Even as a servant, she sets her own terms and keeps them. Now the teaching. There's a Sanskrit line many Hindus know by heart: dharmo rakshati rakshitah. Dharma protects the one who protects it. Dharma is what's right for you to do: your duty, your faithfulness, your truth. Many teachers read Damayanti's road as that line told as a story. Everything a person can lose, she lost. What she wouldn't give up was her dharma, and in the forest, it kept her. Notice what the line doesn't promise. Her road was terrible. It promises that the one thing you guard will guard you back. For today: the line matters most when keeping what's right costs you something, and no one would ever know.

segments.voice: Damayanti had nothing to hold but her dharma. Bring to mind one right thing you're keeping right now, a promise, an honesty, a kindness no one sees, and rest with it as you breathe. If you pray, say dharmo rakshati rakshitah softly and ask for strength to keep guarding it; if not, simply notice what it would cost to let it go, and what it gives you to keep it.
Ashoka, the tree whose name means without sorrow. Damayanti asked it to take hers, and walked on with her dharma whole.
Your line: dharma protects the one who protects it. Damayanti kept hers, and it kept her. See you tomorrow.

793.title: Karkotaka's bite
793.hook: Nala carries a snake king out of a fire, and its bite starts driving out the Kali inside him
793.carry: reciting nala's story is a prayer against kali
793.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's Nala story, the serpent Karkotaka disguises Nala and torments Kali inside him; a verse with the story names Karkotaka, Damayanti, Nala and Rituparna as destroying Kali, and some Hindus still recite it in hard times.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashoka, the tree whose name means without sorrow, and Damayanti alone in the forest with nothing but her dharma. Your line was dharma protects the one who protects it.

A voice in a forest fire. Nala, wandering alone after leaving Damayanti, hears someone calling his name out of the flames. Come quickly, Nala. He follows the voice and finds, curled in the fire, a great serpent. It's Karkotaka, a king among the nagas, and he can't move: a sage's curse has frozen him there until Nala comes to carry him. So the man who lost everything at dice lifts a snake king onto his shoulder and walks out of the fire. And then the snake bites him.
screen: `A VOICE IN THE FIRE.` → `KARKOTAKA, THE SERPENT KING.` → `THEN THE SNAKE BITES HIM.`

segments.voice: Nala's body changes. His beauty is gone; no one would know him now. And Karkotaka explains: my poison won't hurt you. It will torment the one living inside you, the one who brought all this on you. That's Kali. Not the goddess Kali; a different name. This Kali is the spirit of quarrel and bad luck, the same name Hindus give our whole age, the Kali Yuga. Then the serpent gives Nala a plan. Go to King Rituparna of Ayodhya. Call yourself Vahuka and drive his horses, and he'll teach you his secret of dice. And take this garment: when you want your own shape back, put it on and think of me. So the king becomes a charioteer. Every evening he recites a lament for a woman left alone in a forest. Meanwhile, Damayanti has been found and brought home to her father's house and her children. She sends Brahmanas out with one question for every court: where did you go, gambler, after you cut your sleeping wife's cloth? Now the teaching. With this story comes a short Sanskrit verse, still recited, that names four people: Karkotaka the serpent, Damayanti, Nala, and the royal sage Rituparna. Naming them, it says, destroys Kali. Notice who comes first: the snake whose bite began to drive Kali out. Some Hindus still say the verse in a hard season, a lost job, an illness, a run of bad luck. For today: in this tradition, a story isn't only something you hear. Said with faith, it's a prayer.
screen: `THE BITE THAT HIDES HIM.` · `KALI, THE SPIRIT OF BAD LUCK.` · `NALA BECOMES VAHUKA.` · `FOUR NAMES THAT DRIVE OUT KALI.` · then, large: `A STORY, SAID AS A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Say the four names of the verse slowly, one on each breath out: Karkotaka. Damayanti. Nala. Rituparna. Let each one bring back a piece of the story: the bite, the search, the hiding, the secret of dice. If you pray, hold a hard season of your own, or someone else's, in that prayer; if not, simply bring to mind the people who carried you through one.

794.title: Nala forgives
794.hook: a trap made of love brings Nala home, and when Kali finally leaves him, Nala lowers the hand raised to curse
794.howItsDone: The Nala story closes in the Vana Parva with Nala sparing Kali, reuniting with Damayanti, winning back his kingdom and forgiving Pushkara; the sage Brihadashva then gives Yudhishthira the knowledge of dice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karkotaka, whose bite began to drive Kali out, and the verse of four names. Your line was reciting Nala's story is a prayer against Kali.

The answer comes back to Vidarbha. A charioteer in Ayodhya heard Damayanti's question and answered it with a defense of a husband who had lost even his cloth to the birds. Nobody but Nala would know that. So Damayanti sets a trap made of love. She sends word to King Rituparna: Damayanti is choosing a husband again, and the ceremony is tomorrow. Only Nala could get a king there in time, so if Rituparna arrives, she'll know who drove him.
screen: `THE ANSWER COMES BACK.` → `A SWAYAMVARA, TOMORROW.` → `A TRAP MADE OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: Rituparna calls Vahuka, and Nala's heart sinks. Would she really marry again? But he drives, so fast the king's upper cloth blows away. On the road, Rituparna shows off: he glances at a Vibhitaka tree and names exactly how many leaves and fruits it holds. Vahuka cuts it down, counts, and the king is right. So they trade, the secret of dice for the secret of horses. The moment Nala knows the dice, Kali comes out of him, spitting out the serpent's poison. Nala, furious, is ready to curse him. And Kali, trembling, begs: spare me, and those who tell your story will be free of fear from me. Nala lets him go, and Kali slips into the Vibhitaka tree. At Vidarbha there's no ceremony at all. Damayanti knows the thunder of that chariot. She sends their children to the charioteer, and he weeps. The swayamvara, she tells him, was only ever a way to find him. Nala puts on the serpent's garment and is himself again. Later he wins his kingdom back at dice from his brother Pushkara, and then forgives him and sends him home in peace. Now the teaching. Kshama, forgiveness, is one of the great virtues of Hindu dharma. Earlier in the exile, Yudhishthira told Draupadi that forgiveness is truth, forgiveness is sacrifice, and the world is held together by it. Nala lives it twice: he spares the spirit that wrecked his life, and the brother who took his throne. And that promise, made because Nala forgave, stands behind the verse of four names. For today: forgiveness isn't pretending it didn't happen. It's the power to strike back, unused.
screen: `THE RIDE TO VIDARBHA.` · `KALI LEAVES NALA.` · `REUNITED AT VIDARBHA.` · `PUSHKARA SENT HOME IN PEACE.` · then, large: `KSHAMA: FORGIVENESS IS A STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus end their puja with a short prayer asking forgiveness for any mistakes made in it. Bring to mind someone you've been holding something against. You don't have to forgive them yet; just notice the curse you've been holding ready, and loosen your grip on it a little with each breath out. If you pray, ask forgiveness for your own mistakes and strength to give it; if not, simply rest with that open hand.

795.title: Savitri, born of a prayer
795.hook: a king offers the Savitri mantra for years, and the goddess of that prayer gives him a daughter who sees clearly
795.carry: the gayatri: a prayer for light in the mind
795.howItsDone: The story of Savitri and Satyavan is told by the sage Markandeya to Yudhishthira in the Vana Parva; her father prays with the Savitri mantra, the Rig Veda verse to Savitr that most Hindus know as the Gayatri mantra.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vibhitaka, the tree where Kali hid when Nala spared him, and Nala and Damayanti together again. Your line was kshama: forgiveness is a strength.

Has there ever been a woman as devoted as Draupadi? Still in the forest, Yudhishthira puts the question to the sage Markandeya. He has watched her suffer beside him through all of it: the hall, the exile, the forest. Markandeya answers the way Brihadashva did, with a story. There was a princess, he says, named Savitri. And her story, like Nala's, starts long before the trouble does, with a father who wanted a child.
screen: `ANOTHER QUESTION IN THE FOREST.` → `MARKANDEYA TELLS A STORY.` → `A PRINCESS NAMED SAVITRI.`

segments.voice: Ashvapati, king of the Madras, is good, generous and childless. So he takes up a discipline: he eats sparingly, keeps his senses in check, and makes offerings in the fire with the Savitri mantra, for years. At last the goddess of that mantra rises out of the sacred fire and grants him a daughter. He names the girl Savitri, after the goddess who gave her. Now, the teaching hidden in her name. The Savitri mantra is the verse most Hindus know as the Gayatri mantra, chanted after the words om bhur bhuvah svah. It comes from the Rig Veda, and it's addressed to Savitr, the sun as the one who stirs all things to life; that's why it's also called the Savitri. Its heart is one request: may that light inspire our minds. It doesn't ask for wealth, or even for a child. It asks to see clearly. It's taught at the sacred thread ceremony and chanted in many homes at sunrise. So, as many readers notice, the princess of this story is a daughter of the prayer for light. And watch how clearly she sees. She grows so radiant that no man dares to ask for her hand. So her father does something unusual: go yourself, he tells her, and find a husband worthy of you. She travels through forests and hermitages, and comes home with a name. A king called Dyumatsena went blind, lost his kingdom, and lives in a forest hermitage. His son is Satyavan. He's the one I've chosen. For today: when you have to choose, one of the oldest Hindu prayers doesn't say give me what I want. It says light up my mind.
screen: `A FATHER'S LONG DISCIPLINE.` · `THE SAVITRI MANTRA IS THE GAYATRI.` · `"MAY THAT LIGHT INSPIRE OUR MINDS."` · `"GO AND CHOOSE FOR YOURSELF."` · then, large: `A DAUGHTER OF THE PRAYER FOR LIGHT.`

segments.voice: If you know the Gayatri mantra, say it once, slowly, facing whatever light is near you, a window, a lamp, the morning. If you don't know it, ask in your own words for a clear mind about one choice in front of you. If you don't pray, simply sit facing the light, breathe, and let the choice be seen as it is.
Savitri. Named for the goddess of the prayer to the sun, the girl who goes out into the world and sees clearly enough to choose.

796.title: I have chosen once
796.hook: Narada praises the young man Savitri has chosen, then names his one flaw: he will die within a year
796.carry: satya: mind, word and deed as one
796.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, Narada's warning and Savitri's reply, that her mind decided, her words said it and she will act on it, both come before the wedding; Hindus name that agreement of mind, word and deed as satya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Savitri, named for the Gayatri, the prayer for light in the mind. Your line was the gayatri: a prayer for light in the mind.

Savitri has just said his name, and the sage Narada says: oh no. He doesn't mean the young man is bad. Quite the opposite. Ashvapati asks what's wrong with Satyavan, and Narada starts listing what's right. He's truthful. He's generous. He's patient, handsome, kind to everyone. Every good thing you could want. And then the sage stops, and says there's one flaw, and it outweighs all the rest.
screen: `NARADA SAYS: OH NO.` → `EVERYTHING RIGHT ABOUT HIM.` → `AND ONE FLAW.`

segments.voice: The flaw is this, Narada says: a year from today, Satyavan will die. The court goes quiet. Her father turns to Savitri at once: go, choose someone else. And Savitri answers, in the telling, something like this. Some things happen only once. A daughter is given in marriage once. I have chosen once. Whether his life is long or short, I have chosen my husband, and I won't choose twice. My mind decided first, then my words said it, and now I'll act on it. That last line is the teaching. Hindus have a three-word phrase for it: manasa, vacha, karmana. In mind, in word, in deed. When the three agree, that's satya, truth, one of the deepest values in Hindu dharma. Satya isn't only not lying. It's being one person all the way through. Many Hindus end their daily prayers with a verse that offers to God everything done by body, by speech and by mind. And notice the man she chose: Satyavan, whose very name means the truthful one. Narada doesn't argue. Her mind is steady, he tells the king; let it be. He blesses the marriage and goes. Ashvapati travels into the forest to find old blind Dyumatsena, who worries: we live on what the forest gives; how could a princess bear it? She knows all of it, Ashvapati says. 797.title: Savitri's vow
797.hook: in the forest hermitage Savitri counts the days nobody else is counting, and keeps a hard vrata before the last one
797.carry: a vrata is a vow kept with the body
797.howItsDone: In the epic, Savitri keeps her three-night vow standing and fasting just before the day Narada foretold; the Vat Savitri vrata, kept each year by many married Hindu women in the month of Jyeshtha, recalls her story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Satyavan, the truthful one, and Savitri, who chose him in mind, word and deed. Your line was satya: mind, word and deed as one.
screen: `SAVITRI AND SATYAVAN.` · `A CHOICE, AND A WARNING.`

segments.voice: A calendar, kept in one person's head. In the forest hermitage, nobody else is counting. Satyavan gathers fruit and splits wood. His father, a king who lost his sight and then his kingdom, lives there quietly with his wife. Savitri has put away her jewels and wears the rough clothing of the forest. She serves the old couple and speaks gently to everyone. And every day, she counts. The sage Narada said at her father's court that Satyavan would not live out the year. She tells no one. In the epic, those words stay with her day and night.
screen: `A HERMITAGE IN THE FOREST.` → `NARADA'S WORDS, KEPT SILENT.` → `SHE COUNTS THE DAYS.`

segments.voice: As the day draws close, Savitri takes a vow. The epic calls it the triratra, the three-night vow, and she keeps it standing, without food, day and night. Her father-in-law, Dyumatsena, calls it too hard. Savitri answers gently: don't grieve, father. It's resolve that carries a vow through. And the old king, blind and kind, gives way: keep it, then. She doesn't tell him why. She takes the fear she has carried alone and offers it, with her own body. That's a vrata: a vow kept with discipline, often by fasting, offered to God for a purpose. It's one of the most lived parts of Hinduism. Ekadashi fasts, Monday fasts for Shiva, Navaratri fasts: in many Hindu homes, someone is keeping one this week. Tradition says steady discipline like this gathers tapas, a strength that comes from holding firm. And Savitri's vow has a living descendant. Every year, in the month of Jyeshtha, many married Hindu women keep the Vat Savitri vrata: they fast, wind thread around a banyan tree, and hear this very story, praying for their husbands' long lives. On the last night Savitri stands until morning. Then the day itself arrives. She makes her offerings to the fire, and the hermits bless her. The elders urge her to eat at last. She says she'll eat when the sun goes down. For today: a vrata isn't a diet or a punishment. It's love and resolve, kept in the body and offered.

798.title: Yama comes himself
798.hook: Savitri walks into the forest beside Satyavan on the day itself, and Death comes for him in person
798.carry: the body dies; the self is not slain
798.howItsDone: In the Mahabharata's telling, Yama comes for Satyavan in person and draws out a thumb-sized person with his noose, the self the Upanishads describe; the Bhagavad Gita teaches that the self is not slain when the body is.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vrata, Savitri's three-night vow, the root of a fast women still keep. Your line was a vrata is a vow kept with the body.

Satyavan shoulders his axe. He's heading into the woods for fruit and firewood, as he does every morning. And Savitri, who has eaten nothing through her vow, asks to come along. He's surprised. You've never come before, he says; the path is hard, and you're weak from fasting. She won't be talked out of it. She even asks his parents' leave, and they give it. So the two of them set off together, and the epic says she looks cheerful while her heart is burning.
screen: `AN AXE AND A FOREST PATH.` → `SHE ASKS TO COME ALONG.` → `CHEERFUL, WITH A BURNING HEART.`

segments.voice: Satyavan shows her the forest as they walk, the streams and the flowering trees. He gathers fruit and starts to split wood. Then he stops. His head aches, he says. He wants to lie down. Savitri sits on the ground and takes his head into her lap. And then she sees someone: a tall figure, dark, dressed in red, a noose in his hand, standing over Satyavan. She lays her husband's head down gently, stands, joins her palms and asks who he is. He is Yama, lord of death, and Satyavan's time has come. Why have you come yourself, she asks, and not your messengers? Because Satyavan was good, Yama answers, not someone to be fetched by servants. And with his noose he draws out of Satyavan's body a person no bigger than a thumb. Now the teaching in that detail. The Upanishads describe the self within each of us as a person the size of a thumb. What Yama takes is not the body; the body lies still on the ground. What leaves is the self, the one who lived in it. This is the Hindu view of death: the body dies, and the self is not slain. The Bhagavad Gita says it plainly: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves a worn-out body and takes another. And Yama is also called Dharmaraja, king of dharma: in this tradition, death keeps a just order. So Yama turns south with what he's taken. And Savitri does what no one does. She follows. For today: when someone dies, Hindus grieve, and also hold this: the one we loved was never only the body.
